introduction.description.value: This short, interactive activity will guide you through the methods and techniques of the cloud, from its foundations to its deployment.

introduction.part1.description.value: Tackle 'Myth vs. Fact' questions about what the cloud really is.

introduction.part2.description.value: Play a drag-and-drop game to sort IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS.

introduction.part3.description.value: Solve real-world scenarios to understand Public, Private, and Hybrid clouds.

part1.question1.explanation.value: That's right! The cloud's central innovation is placing large numbers of servers in data centers, typically located far from the individuals and organizations that access them.

part1.question1.statement.value: The foundations of cloud computing are high-powered computers called servers, located in facilities called data centers.

part1.question2.explanation.value: Exactly. Historically, organizations operated their own on-premises equipment. Cloud computing allows them to access resources remotely from a cloud provider instead.

part1.question2.statement.value: Cloud computing requires organizations to buy and operate their own computer equipment on-premises.

part1.subtitle.value: Is the following statement a myth or a fact?

part2.example1.correct.value: You got it. Scalable storage is a core component of infrastructure that you rent from a provider. This is a classic IaaS offering.

part2.example1.hint.paas.value: While a PaaS application would *use* storage, the storage service itself is a more fundamental building block. It's part of the core infrastructure.

part2.example1.hint.saas.value: This isn't a complete application, but a raw component you'd use to build one. Which model provides these fundamental building blocks?

part2.example1.text.value: Paying for storage space that automatically scales to match the amount of data in use.

part2.example2.correct.value: That's it! These are examples of complete software products that you access, typically by paying a subscription. This is Software as a Service.

part2.example2.hint.iaas.value: With Zoom or Slack, are you managing servers or just using an app? IaaS is about renting the servers themselves. This is a level above that.

part2.example2.hint.paas.value: PaaS is a platform for developers to *create* apps. Zoom is an app that has already been created for you to use. Which model fits that description?

part2.example2.text.value: Using Zoom for video calls or Slack for messaging.

part2.example3.correct.value: Perfect! With PaaS, you focus on your application code, while the provider handles the underlying infrastructure and technical responsibilities, like server maintenance.

part2.example3.hint.iaas.value: You're getting warmer! IaaS would give you the server, but you would be responsible for maintaining it. This service handles that maintenance for you.

part2.example3.hint.saas.value: This is a model for *running* your own software, not for *using* someone else's. Which category provides that kind of platform?

part2.example3.text.value: Operating your own software in the cloud while a provider handles and maintains the servers.

part2.example4.correct.value: Correct! A file sharing service is a ready-to-use application provided for end-users, which is the definition of SaaS.

part2.example4.hint.iaas.value: File sharing is a feature of a complete software product. IaaS would be renting the raw storage where those files are kept.

part2.example4.hint.paas.value: You are *using* a finished service, not *building* one. PaaS is the environment for building. What's the model for using?

part2.example4.text.value: Accessing a file sharing service to collaborate with a team.

part2.example5.correct.value: Exactly! You are renting the provider's fundamental computing resources (their infrastructure) to perform complex tasks. This is IaaS.

part2.example5.hint.paas.value: PaaS provides a managed platform, but when you're directly utilizing raw processing power and storage for custom analytics, you're using the underlying infrastructure.

part2.example5.hint.saas.value: This describes using core computing power, not a specific, pre-built software application. Which model is about renting raw resources?

part2.example5.text.value: Using a provider's infrastructure for large-scale data processing and analytics.

part2.example6.correct.value: That's right. When you deploy and run your own software and tools on a managed environment from a cloud provider, that's Platform as a Service.

part2.example6.hint.iaas.value: You could do this with IaaS, but you'd also have to manage the operating systems and servers. PaaS handles that for you so you can focus on your app.

part2.example6.hint.saas.value: This is about running your *own* custom application, not subscribing to one made by someone else. Which model provides a platform for your own software?

part2.example6.text.value: Hosting your company's custom application and its business analytics tools.

part2.hint.default.value: That doesn't seem to be the right fit. Think about the level of management provided by the service.

part2.subtitle.value: Drag each example to the correct service model category.

part3.explanation.default.value: That's a good thought, but there's a better fit. Consider the key requirements of the scenario.

part3.scenario1.explanation.value: A Private Cloud is ideal here. It offers the greatest security by imposing more restrictions on access, making it suitable for sensitive information like financial records or proprietary research.

part3.scenario1.text.value: A financial firm needs to store proprietary research with greater security, requiring an encrypted VPN connection for its employees to access it.

part3.scenario2.explanation.value: A Public Cloud is the perfect choice. They are called 'public' because nearly any customer can pay to use their servers, making them cheaper and offering easy access.

part3.scenario2.text.value: A software company wants to deploy its app for nearly any customer to use, with easy access over standard internet connections and lower costs.

part3.scenario3.explanation.value: This is a classic Hybrid Cloud. This model involves splitting data and applications across public and private clouds to combine the benefits of both.

part3.scenario3.text.value: A company runs its videoconferencing software on a public cloud but stores its sensitive customer service records in a separate, more secure environment.

part3.subtitle.value: Read the scenario and choose the most appropriate cloud model.

part3.venn.caption.value: Visual representation: Hybrid Cloud combines Public and Private clouds

part4.aws.model.label.value: AWS provides raw infrastructure as Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS)

part4.aws.provide1.value: Physical servers, storage, and networking hardware

part4.aws.provide2.value: On-demand processing power and data storage

part4.aws.provide3.value: Global data centers with redundancy and uptime

part4.aws.service.value: Service Model: Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)

part4.insight.value: Key Insight: AWS provides IaaS (servers and infrastructure) → Netflix uses that as PaaS (platform to build their service) → You experience it as SaaS (ready-to-use software). The same physical infrastructure serves three different roles!

part4.instructions.value: Click the buttons below to switch between AWS's infrastructure layer, Netflix's platform layer, and the subscriber's application layer:

part4.intro.description.value: To the user Netflix is an intentionally simple app. You open it, browse shows, and start watching. Behind that experience is a complex cloud computing system involving multiple layers of technology and different companies working together.

part4.intro.instruction.value: Click each tab below to see the behind-the-scenes view from each perspective. You'll need to explore all three to continue.

part4.intro.purpose.value: In this activity, you'll explore Netflix service from three different perspectives: the cloud infrastructure provider (AWS), the platform operator (Netflix), and you, the subscriber.

part4.misconceptions.item1.value: PaaS and SaaS aren't different products—they're different perspectives on how the same infrastructure is used.

part4.misconceptions.item2.value: The cloud provider (like AWS) provides IaaS to Netflix, who builds PaaS on top of it, then offers SaaS to you.

part4.misconceptions.item3.value: You don't need to know the layers below your role—subscribers don't need to understand PaaS or IaaS.

part4.misconceptions.item4.value: The same infrastructure can be IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS simultaneously, depending on who is using it and how.

part5.deployment.public.blurb.value: Elastic capacity with pay‑as‑you‑go. Great for spiky workloads and faster global reach.

part5.deployment.sustainability.value: Large public clouds often run in hyperscale data centers that concentrate efficiency—but all data centers consume significant electricity and cooling water; impact depends on grid mix and cooling approach.

part5.primer.point1.value: Cloud computing means remote servers in data centers handle storage and processing. You access those resources over the internet.

part5.primer.point2.value: Service models differ by who runs what: IaaS (rent servers), PaaS (run your app on the provider's platform), SaaS (use their app).

part5.primer.point3.value: Deployment models: public (multi-tenant data centers), private (single-tenant), hybrid (mix of both).

part5.role.text.value: You're the cloud architect. Design the best solution for this client.

part5.saas.disabled.value: SaaS is not available for this scenario because the requirements specify custom software development.

part5.scenario1.description.value: You're a small team launching a new consumer app. User growth is uncertain and potentially spiky. You need to ship fast and keep costs sensible at low/medium scale.

part5.scenario2.description.value: A healthcare provider needs to store and process PHI. Compliance and control matter most, but the portal must still scale during seasonal surges.

part5.scenario3.description.value: A simple app that lets salespeople log customers, notes, and deals so managers can see progress. ~500–5,000 employees will use it.

part5.scenario3.title.value: Customer-tracking tool for a sales team (a 'CRM')

part5.service.heading.value: 1) Choose a Service Model for this scenario

part5.service.iaas.blurb.value: You manage OS/runtime and scaling. Highest control and flexibility; slower to ship; more ops work.

part5.service.paas.blurb.value: You push code; platform handles runtime, scaling, and much of ops. Good balance of speed and control.

part5.service.saas.blurb.value: You subscribe to software someone else runs. Fastest time‑to‑value; least control/customization.

part5.steps.3.value: Choose one Deployment Model for this scenario (where it runs).

summary.description.value: You've completed the introduction to how cloud computing works. Here's a quick recap of what you learned.

summary.recap.application.text.value: When designing cloud solutions, consider security needs, cost constraints, and how usage might change over time.

summary.recap.foundations.text.value: The cloud is a physical network of servers in data centers, accessed remotely.

summary.recap.hybrid.value: - Hybrid combines public and private clouds for flexibility.

summary.recap.iaas.value: - IaaS is renting a provider's cloud infrastructure (servers, storage).

summary.recap.paas.value: - PaaS is a platform to operate your own software on, where the provider handles the servers.

summary.recap.perspective.text.value: The same infrastructure can be different service models depending on your role (Netflix uses PaaS, subscribers use SaaS).

summary.recap.private.value: - Private is dedicated to a single customer for greater security and control.

summary.recap.public.value: - Public is shared, cost-effective, and easily accessible.

summary.recap.saas.value: - SaaS is paying to access another organization's ready-to-use software.
